hypothesis: Question: do older (2011 start-up regime) hourly records help or hurt transfer to a later period when the model is otherwise fixed? Evidence so far: the development leader idea-a0bc19 (plain Poisson HGB, all features, uniform weights) scored loss 54.01 / group MAE 35.89 with pred_mean 264.3 vs train_last60_mean 232.5; its child idea-2a518e imposed an explicit exponential YoY growth factor (selected damp 1.0, implied factor 1.068 at eval mid, pred_mean 296.5) and got worse (65.18 / 41.55), so explicit level extrapolation overshot even though its internal folds preferred it. Both programs' internal spring fold (cut ~425) showed about -100 bias for every variant, i.e. a level jump no candidate captured, which makes the internal fold mean a weak selector. This changed my view: instead of extrapolating a trend, test whether de-emphasizing the early-2011 regime (recency sample weights with half-life in {none,365,180,90} days, weights normalized to mean 1, identical hparams and features to idea-a0bc19) lets the tree model learn a level/profile closer to the recent regime without extrapolation. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if 2011 relationships transfer well, hl_none wins internally and dev loss stays ~54 -- an informative negative result that the full history is worth keeping; (B) if the ramp-up regime distorts learned levels, hl_180 or hl_90 wins internally and dev loss drops below 54 with pred_mean modestly above 264; (C) a possible regression: weighting shrinks effective sample size (reported per fold) and could raise variance, giving worse dev RMSE even if internal folds favor it, as happened with idea-2a518e. Selection is by mean RMSE over 3 chronological 61-day-horizon folds with ties resolved toward uniform weights; the program reports the selected half-life, per-fold results, effective sample sizes and any fallback. Single-factor design: only sample weights vary.
